artifacts.delta_brief: Change: In 2023, KO expands the macro backdrop from a general inflation/recession list to explicitly flag interest-rate conditions, bank failures, and tax-rule approaches as potential shocks to liquidity and demand (2022 para 1; 2023 para 1). Geopolitical exposure is reframed from a Russia-Ukraine centered disruption narrative to a broader multi-conflict posture that includes Middle East instability and added security risk to people and infrastructure (2022 para 5; 2023 para 6). Drivers: The 2022 conflict discussion emphasizes second-order knock-ons like commodity volatility, supply chain disruption, cyber exposure, sanctions and export controls, and employee-safety and labor impacts (2022 para 5), while 2023 generalizes the same mechanism to international conflicts as a recurring operating condition with similar cost, logistics, cyber and IP-enforcement consequences (2023 para 7). The supply chain risk stack remains an amplifier, with 2022 detailing climate- and agriculture-linked input volatility that can compound inflation and logistics constraints (2022 para 15), and 2023 reiterating that conflict-driven disruptions and higher input costs can pressure availability and margins (2023 para 7). Separately, 2023 introduces acquisition integration and control-extension risk as an additional pathway to operational disruption and negative publicity, broadening the risk set beyond exogenous macro and geopolitical drivers (2023 para 20). Caveat: Both years include explicit uncertainty and materiality qualifiers around conflict impacts, so wording shifts may reflect expanded scenario coverage rather than realized losses to date (2022 para 5; 2023 para 8). Focuspack is a subset; verify in full compare pane.
